archetype.name: Retooling Year (a real .500 team)
archetype.definition: Miami repeated last year's near-.500 record, but this time the run differential backed it up, showing a roster that improved underneath a flat result without becoming a contender.

report.headline: Same record as 2025, but this time the .500 was earned

recap.finish: 80-82, third in the NL East, 14 games behind Atlanta; missed the postseason
recap.body:
On the surface the 2026 Marlins look like a rerun: 80-82 after 79-83. The difference is what sits under the record. Last year's team was outscored by roughly 89 runs and won about seven games more than that margin implied. This year's team scored 715 and allowed 712, a +0.02 Run Diff / G, and finished a game and change short of what that margin implied. The site ranked it 14th of 30, up from 22nd. The record stood still, but the club behind it got better.

The season came in three stretches, and only one of them was good. A 4-1 opening week gave way to an 11-15 April and an 11-18 May, putting them at 26-34 by the end of May. Somewhere in the early going sat a 12-game losing streak. Then June happened: 20-6 with 133 runs scored and 80 allowed, a +53 month that pulled them to 46-40. It didn't last. They went 10-15 in July and were back to 56-55, then played .500 ball the rest of the way. Outside June they were 60-76 and outscored by 50, which tells you the hot month was the exception, not the team's true level.

The strength was the lineup, graded A- and carried by Otto Lopez. He hit .305 with 34 steals and a 115 wRC+ and added 10.2 Def Runs at shortstop. His 5.9 WAR was more than double any teammate's, and he ranked third among 51 shortstops on the site. Javier Sanoja (115 wRC+) and Griffin Conine (133 wRC+ in 323 PA) gave real production, and Heriberto Hernández and Kyle Stowers added 46 home runs between them. But the team's .726 OPS ranked 9th while its runs per game ranked only 18th. The lineup reached base and hit for some power without cashing it in, and Owen Caissie's -0.5 WAR in 330 PA, with -7.5 Def Runs in the outfield, was a hole.

The bigger change was run prevention. Team ERA fell from 4.60 to 4.09, and the Def Rank climbed from 26th to 13th. Sandy Alcantara gave 214 innings at a 3.87 ERA. Max Meyer was the best arm, an All-Star with a 2.68 ERA, but over only 111 innings. Eury Pérez missed bats (25.8 K %) but walked 10.3% of hitters. The bullpen was the weak group at C-. Michael Petersen and Calvin Faucher were solid setup men with 44 holds between them. Victor Vodnik (4.91 ERA) and Cade Gibson (5.36) leaked runs behind them, and no reliever in the top five reached five saves.

They closed 6-4 and took two of three from the division-champion Braves in the final weekend, but they were never really in the race. They finished eight games behind Philadelphia and 14 behind Atlanta. This was a team that earned its record honestly, which last year's could not claim.

highlights.title: Run prevention climbed from 26th to 13th
highlights.body: Team ERA dropped by half a run, from 4.60 to 4.09, and the Def Rank jumped 13 spots. Alcantara's 214 innings and Meyer's 2.68 ERA anchored it. Because the gain came from a deeper rotation rather than fielding (Fielding Runs were about average), it looks repeatable as long as those arms stay healthy.

highlights.title: Otto Lopez carried the A- lineup
highlights.body: Lopez hit .305 with 34 steals and 10.2 Def Runs at short, good for 5.9 WAR and an All-Star nod. The lineup's grade leans heavily on him; the next-best hitter, Sanoja, posted 2.9 WAR. Sanoja and Conine both posted wRC+ of 115 or better, so there is a supporting cast, but Lopez is the engine.

highlights.title: The record was finally honest
highlights.body: After two winning-adjacent seasons (2023 and 2025) built on beating the run differential by 9.1 and 6.7 wins, this team's +0.02 per-game margin matched its record almost exactly. An 80-82 team with a break-even differential is a sturdier base than a 79-83 team that was outscored by nearly 90 runs.

lowlights.title: One great month, five mediocre ones
lowlights.body: June's 20-6 accounted for the whole positive run differential. The rest of the year was 60-76, and a 12-game losing streak buried the early season. A team that needs a month like that just to reach .500 is not yet a contender.

lowlights.title: OPS didn't turn into runs
lowlights.body: A .726 team OPS ranked 9th, yet the offense was only 18th in runs per game. Some of that gap is sequencing and may even out. Some of it is a lineup with plenty of on-base, speed and scattered power that never clustered its production.

lowlights.title: A C- bullpen behind the setup men
lowlights.body: Petersen (30.1 K %) and Faucher (2.95 FIP) were reliable. The rest of the top five's innings went to Vodnik, Gibson and King, whose ERAs ran from 3.99 to 5.36. Gibson's 3.99 FIP suggests some bad luck, but King's 4.87 FIP says his 3.99 ERA flattered him.

arc.note: They sank to 26-34 through May, surged to 46-40 on a 20-6 June, then gave it back with a 10-15 July and played .500 ball to the finish.

recap.nextYear: The foundation is real: a break-even run differential, a top-half run prevention unit, and an A- lineup. Lopez is its centerpiece, with Sanoja and Conine as productive complements. Several numbers point to regression or upside. Tyler Phillips' 3.34 ERA sits against a 4.65 FIP and is likely to rise. Meyer's 2.68 ERA came in just 111 innings, so a full season from him would be a major gain. Pérez's walks (10.3 BB %) are what stand between him and a top-of-rotation line. The bullpen behind Petersen and Faucher is the clearest group to upgrade, and Caissie's negative-WAR season marks the weakest lineup spot. Luck was neutral this year (-1.3 W vs Run Diff), so unlike 2023 and 2025 there's no cushion to give back. Any jump has to come from the roster getting better, not the bounces.

confidence.note: Full 162-game season; record and run differential agree.
